## The idea

A note drawn one staff step higher moves to the next letter name. That step may
span one semitone or two. The page uses a diatonic coordinate system, where lines
and spaces count letters. MIDI uses a chromatic coordinate system, where every
integer counts one semitone. Confusing the two turns a visual step into the wrong
pitch.

The *staff* has five lines and four spaces. A *treble clef* assigns G4 to the
second line from the bottom. Once that anchor is known, every adjacent position
follows the repeating letters A through G. Middle C sits on a short ledger line
below the staff. Treat it as coordinate zero and the bottom treble line, E4,
becomes coordinate two.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 90
use_synth :piano

letters = [:c, :d, :e, :f, :g, :a, :b]
semitones = {c: 0, d: 2, e: 4, f: 5, g: 7, a: 9, b: 11}

define :staff_record do |position, letters, semitones|
  letter = letters[position % 7]
  octave = 4 + (position / 7).floor
  midi = 12 * (octave + 1) + semitones[letter]
  {position: position, letter: letter, octave: octave, midi: midi}
end

# Eight printed positions: bottom line through the space above the staff.
printed_positions = [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]

printed_positions.each do |position|
  record = staff_record(position, letters, semitones)
  puts "position #{position}: #{record[:letter]}#{record[:octave]} midi=#{record[:midi]}"
  play record[:midi], release: 0.55
  sleep 0.75
end

# One-octave cheat sheet from middle C to the next C.
(0..7).each { |position| puts staff_record(position, letters, semitones) }
```

The eight positions rise E4, F4, G4, A4, B4, C5, D5, F5 with E5 included at
position nine? Read the log carefully: positions two through nine actually give
E4 through F5 in consecutive letters. Their MIDI gaps alternate between one and
two semitones even though every drawn move is one staff step.

## Change one thing

1. Replace the positions with `[0, 2, 4, 6]`. These are middle C and every other
   diatonic note. The visual skips produce a C-major seventh chord when played
   together.
2. Play positions `2` and `3` repeatedly. E to F is one staff step and one
   semitone. Compare positions `3` and `4`, F to G, where the same visual step
   spans two semitones.
3. Add negative positions `-1` and `-2`. Ruby's modulo and floor division keep
   the letter and octave sequence working below middle C.

## Why it works

The letter cycle is a seven-element ring. Position modulo seven selects a letter.
Floor division by seven counts completed letter cycles and adjusts the octave.
The semitone hash performs the separate conversion from diatonic name to
chromatic distance inside C major.

Treble clef is an offset convention. It gives one printed line a known pitch,
which determines all others. Memorising E-G-B-D-F and F-A-C-E can help with
spot checks, but the coordinate model explains ledger lines and prevents lines
and spaces from becoming unrelated tables.

Accidentals and key signatures will modify the final semitone lookup in Lesson
40. They do not move the note head to another staff coordinate. F-sharp and F
occupy the same line or space because both retain the letter F.

The printed shape also carries duration through note heads, stems, beams, and
dots. This lesson deliberately ignores those marks so vertical position remains
the only changing field. When rhythm returns in Lesson 41, pitch coordinate and
duration will enter separate event keys. Keeping them separate prevents a dense
eighth-note beam from becoming part of the pitch decoder.

## Take it further

Generate a Markdown cheat sheet for positions `-2` through `9`. Each row must
contain coordinate, line-or-space classification, letter, octave, Sonic Pi
symbol, and MIDI integer. Mark middle C and the five treble staff lines. Then
enter eight note-head positions from a printed source and play the decoded
sequence without copying note names from another transcription.
